161	Risk_Stratification_Engine 2.0 GB and ForcePlate_DecisionSystem 1.6 GB.
162	
163	Remaining: `ERROR (2 errors)` = `rsync-timeout` + `snapshot:sessions`, which are the same
164	single `codex/sessions` wedge counted twice (the watchdog error plus the snapshot failure
165	it causes). Not two problems. Clear `.errors.log` only after the wedge itself is fixed.
166	
167	Verification trap met here: `find -newermt '-30 minutes'` silently matches nothing on BSD
168	find (macOS) — it wants an absolute date. Use `find -newer <reference-file>` instead. Also
169	remember `rsync -a` preserves source mtimes, so freshly-copied files look old; compare
170	*directory* mtimes or use a reference file to prove a capture ran.
171	
172	Note the run ordering: Drive SNAPs run *before* the SSD capture, so a long `codex/sessions`
173	seed delays the SSD layer within a given run. Not a failure, just a wait.
174	
175	## `snapshot:sessions` — evidence from a live reproduction, 2026-08-14 15:20 (stack-doctor)
176	
177	Caught the hang in progress and narrowed it. **Root cause still open** — this section is
178	evidence, not a verdict. Everything below is measured, not inferred:
179	
180	- **It is a hang, not a slow transfer.** Four rsync processes (client `-a ... codex/sessions/`,
181	  its `--server` receiver, plus two older receivers) sat at **0.01–0.03 s of CPU across
182	  34–85 minutes** of wall clock. Zero progress, not slow progress.
183	- **Nothing is left to copy.** The mirror is **256/256 files** — the previously-missing
184	  `2026/08/06/rollout-*.jsonl` is present. A complete mirror still hangs.
185	- **The mount is healthy.** A recursive `find` over the destination returned 256 files
186	  promptly, and `touch` inside the exact hung directory succeeded instantly. Reads *and*
187	  writes both work, so this is not a wedged DriveFS/FUSE mount.
188	- **The wedged processes ignore SIGTERM** (still alive minutes later in `S` state) — they
189	  are blocked inside a call that neither returns nor delivers signals.
190	- **Dry runs cannot see it**: `-n` completes clean, live runs hang. Another instance of the
191	  "`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path" trap above.
192	
193	### Orphans are a symptom, not the cause
194	
195	Two `rsync --server` receivers were **orphaned to PPID 1** (started 13:55 and 14:33). It is
196	tempting to call them the blocker; the timeline refutes it — the **10:31:54 run hung at the
197	identical point** (last line `SNAP skip (missing): .codex/memories`, no end line) while the
198	oldest surviving orphan did not exist until 13:55. `kill` on both orphans did not unblock
199	the live pair either.
200	
201	Why they accumulate: **`daily-backup.ps1` contains no `pkill` at all** (verified by grep —
202	do not go looking for one). The anchored `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` belongs to an *ad-hoc
203	wrapper used interactively in another session*. That pattern matches only the client, whose
204	`argv[0]` is the full path; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`, so
205	`pgrep -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` returns the client alone. Every kill-and-retry therefore strands
206	one more receiver. If that wrapper is reused, match on `-x rsync` or the destination path.
207	
208	### ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-14 17:00 — it is not rsync
209	
210	Ran the copy in the foreground with `-avv`, unpiped. It printed ~99 lines of
211	`... is uptodate` and froze mid-filename. Then:
212	
213	- `sample <receiver-pid>` showed the process blocked in **`__mmap`** — one frame, not moving.
214	- `lsof` on it showed FD 5 open on a specific **destination** file:
215	  `codex/sessions/2026/05/08/rollout-2026-05-08T17-14-58-019e09a8-*.jsonl`.
216	- **`head -c 512` on that destination file hangs by itself**, with zero rsync processes
217	  running. A plain read. So the file is unreadable through DriveFS.
218	- A 44-file sample elsewhere in the same mirror read instantly, so it is **specific files,
219	  not the mount**.
220	
221	The files are **DriveFS placeholders** — uploaded to Google, then evicted from the local
222	cache. Census of the destination on 2026-08-14: 256 files, **122 materialized (48.5 MB on
223	disk), 134 placeholder-only (240.7 MB logical, 0 bytes local)**. Source is 256/256
224	materialized. Detect with `stat -f '%b %z'`: blocks==0 with a nonzero logical size means
225	the content is not local. Reading one forces an on-demand fetch, and that fetch stalls —
226	which is what blocks `__mmap`. rsync was the victim, not the cause. **Do not chase rsync
227	flags**; the block happens at open, before any comparison strategy applies.
228	
229	**This inverts the problem: the backup is fine, the verification is what's broken.** All
230	256 files are on Google's servers. Nothing is missing. What fails is the *next* run's
231	attempt to re-read them to confirm they match. Never conclude "the snapshot is broken"
232	from this failure mode.
233	
234	Also: `du -sh` on the destination reports the *local cache* (48 MB), not the logical 289 MB.
235	Both numbers are true and mean different things — do not treat the gap as missing data.
236	
237	Diagnostic sequence that worked, reuse it: `sample <pid>` for the blocking syscall →
238	`lsof -p <pid>` for the file it is on → bounded `head -c` on that path to prove the
239	filesystem, not the tool, is at fault.
240	
241	**Attempted fix that DID NOT WORK**: pinning `My Drive/Backups` "Available offline" via the
242	Finder context menu (there is no CLI or xattr for it — the app ships no control surface).
243	Eric pinned it 2026-08-14 17:30. Result: **one** file materialized, then flat for 5 minutes
244	(133 placeholders, 49.2 MB, unchanged). Restarting Drive did not help either.
245	
246	**DriveFS on this Mac is itself unhealthy** — this is the real blocker, not rsync and not
247	the pin:
248	- It refused a graceful `osascript quit` for 20s and needed SIGKILL. Its log emitted
249	  `crashpad ... ThreadsStuck` every 6s. Restarting cleared the stuck threads but nothing else.
250	- The **download** queue fails, not just uploads: `merger.cc:969:ProcessDownloadEvent` +
251	  `HandleFailedChange [DownloadMergeQueueItem]`. DriveFS cannot pull content *down*.
252	- Signs of local DB damage: `item_query_handler.cc:1135:OnGetItemIds Ignoring item
253	  local-376561 that's missing from ...`.
254	- NOT quota: 671 GB used of 5.5 TB.
255	
256	**Do not clear the DriveFS content cache as the remedy.** It converts every materialized
257	file into a placeholder needing re-download, feeding the exact mechanism that is failing —
258	122 readable files could become 0. If DriveFS is repaired, do it by signing out and back in
259	to force a DB rebuild, deliberately, with time to watch it.
260	
261	### RESOLVED 2026-08-14 — the backup was never broken, the verification was
262	
263	**Final mechanism**: files Drive has evicted from local cache are placeholders. Fetching a
264	placeholder through DriveFS is *unreliable* — usually fast, sometimes stalling for tens of
265	minutes. rsync blocking on such a fetch is the entire "wedge". Proof it is a slow fetch and
266	not a poisoned file: the file that hung four separate times **now reads instantly**, and its
267	blocks went 0 → 770,048 — the repeated read attempts eventually completed the fetch. Six
268	other placeholders read fine first try. Nothing was corrupt.
269	
270	**`~/.claude/scripts/verify-drive-backup.sh` (`0d2edb5`) is now the way to verify.** It
271	compares the Drive API's server-side `md5Checksum` against a local md5 — metadata only, no
272	DriveFS read, batched ~25 names per query. First run on `~/.codex/sessions`:
273	**256/256 verified, 0 mismatch, 0 missing.** The snapshot that logged `FAILED` for days was
274	complete and byte-correct the whole time.
275	
276	Do not "fix" this by deleting Drive copies. Both files that hung were verified byte-identical
277	to source *before* anything was touched — deleting would have destroyed a good backup to
278	repair a read path.
279	
280	**It is plain fetch latency, scaling with file size** — no mystery left. A full read-scan of
281	all 256 files with a 6s per-file cap: 33 stalled, and those averaged **2,301 KB vs 1,156 KB
282	for the set overall** (max 15.8 MB). Bigger file, longer fetch. Nothing file-specific,
283	nothing corrupt. The scan itself moved the mirror from 122 → 230 materialized (48.5 → 161.8 MB
284	local), which is exactly what "reading materializes it" predicts.
285	
286	Caution when testing this: **reading a file materializes it**, so any scan warms the cache and
287	a later run passes for reasons that will not hold once Drive evicts again. Timestamp results
288	and never treat a post-scan rsync run as a clean verification.
289	
290	### Why DriveFS is unhealthy — found 2026-08-14 18:20
291	
292	**Google Drive is mirroring `~/DEV` as a device-backup folder named "My Mac"**, including
293	**34 `.git` directories / 3,470 files**. VS Code has `"git.autofetch": true`, which rewrites
294	every repo's `FETCH_HEAD` on a 180s cycle; Drive uploads all 34 each time. That is the source
295	of the `PRECONDITION_FAILED` storms on `FETCH_HEAD` and the stuck threads in `drive_fs.txt`,
296	and therefore of the slow placeholder fetches upstream.
297	
298	Proof (not inference): local `~/DEV/*/.git/FETCH_HEAD` all stamped 18:22:09 while Drive's
299	server copies read `2026-08-14T23:22:09Z` — same second — and the Drive parent chain resolves
300	`FETCH_HEAD → .git → DataBase_GPS_Reporting → DEV → My Mac`.
301	
302	**`OneDrive-Import` was a red herring** — it holds 22 `.git` dirs / 7,292 files, but they are
303	static archives and do not churn. Don't chase it.
304	
305	**FIXED 2026-08-14 ~18:28 — Eric removed `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders from your
306	computer" (keeping the cloud copy). Verified, and it worked:**
307	- Server-side `FETCH_HEAD` froze at `23:28:12Z` while local `~/DEV` copies kept updating
308	  (18:32:28) — churn decoupled, `git.autofetch` left ON as intended.
309	- `PRECONDITION_FAILED` 14 → **0**. `ProcessDownloadEvent` errors 11 → **0**.
310	  `HandleFailedChange` stable (idle retry backlog, not growing).
311	- Google Drive CPU **64.6% → 0.0%**.
312	- **End-to-end: 5/5 genuine placeholders (blocks==0) fetched in 2–3s each**, where the same
313	  class of read previously stalled for minutes or indefinitely. This is the actual cure for
314	  the `snapshot:sessions` wedge — the watchdog only bounded it.
315	
316	Original recommendation, for the record: remove `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders
317	from your computer", choosing KEEP for the existing cloud copy. The mirror is redundant and
318	strictly worse than the nightly, which already covers `~/DEV` via 68 manifest entries →
319	SSD + GitHub with `.git` excluded and credential files denied (6 projects hit that policy on
320	2026-08-14). **Do not** "fix" this by disabling `git.autofetch`: that masks the symptom, costs
321	a useful feature, and leaves 3,470 `.git` files still mirrored to churn on every commit and
322	checkout. Verify afterward by re-querying `FETCH_HEAD` modifiedTime via the Drive API and
323	re-checking `drive_fs.txt` for `ThreadsStuck` / `PRECONDITION_FAILED`.
324	
325	How to check whether anything is pending before any Drive surgery: sample
326	`grep -c HandleModifiedLocalItem/HandleFailedChange/DownloadMergeQueueItem` in
327	`~/Library/Application Support/Google/DriveFS/Logs/drive_fs.txt` over ~90s — flat counters
328	mean idle queues. **Do not** use the presence of `com.google.drivefs.item-id` as an
329	upload-pending signal: 774 files in Backups lacked it and were all already on the server.
330	
331	Rejected: `--ignore-existing` (would freeze any mid-session rollout file at its partial
332	size in Drive permanently) and leaving the watchdog to absorb it (~15 min wasted nightly,
333	and two standing errors would camouflage real ones).
334	
335	Note `-W` (whole-file) is already default for local transfers, so `--whole-file`,
336	`--size-only` and delta-algorithm tuning are all dead ends here — the block happens on
337	open, before any comparison strategy matters.
338	
339	## The SSD layer's real failure mode — schedule/mount mismatch, found 2026-08-29
340	
341	**The nightly is healthy; the SSD layer is simply absent at run time.** `com.keystone.dailybackup`
342	fires at 00:30 and CRASHBOX is normally unplugged then, so every run logs
343	`TARGET SSD /Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup NOT MOUNTED - orphan and working-tree capture
344	SKIPPED this run` and ends `OK (0 errors)`. A clean exit code is therefore **not** evidence the
345	SSD captured — the skip is not an error. Check `_receipts/run-*.txt` mtime on the drive instead.
346	
347	Receipt history proves the pattern: 10 SSD captures total, clustered on days the drive happened
348	to be attached (Aug 6, Aug 14 ×5, Aug 15, Aug 16, Aug 17), then a **12-day gap** to Aug 29. Eric
349	read this as "the SSD backup has never run"; it had, just rarely.
350	
351	**Manual run is the remedy and takes ~6 minutes**, not the ~45 the 2026-08-14 notes imply:
352	`/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh -File ~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (no SSD-only switch exists; do
353	not add one). Run 20260829-073713: Drive SNAPs finished in **6 seconds** — the `codex/sessions`
354	wedge is genuinely gone since the `~/DEV` de-mirroring fix — DEV capture 07:37–07:40, `.claude`/
355	`.codex`/`.gemini`/SecondBrain state 07:41–07:42, `RECEIPT ssd : verified` at 07:42:50,
356	`end: OK (0 errors)` at 07:43:14. SSD 25 → 27 GB. The long tail in the 00:34 nightly was the
357	memsearch INDEX step (00:51→01:18), which runs *after* the backup and is not part of it.
358	
359	Verification trap repeated here: **top-level SSD directory mtimes stay old after a successful
360	capture** (`SecondBrain` still read Aug 17, `claude` Aug 14) because `rsync -a` preserves source
361	mtimes and a parent dir's mtime only moves when an entry is added or removed at that level. The
362	`STATE-SSD ... : OK` log lines and the receipt are the evidence; mtimes are not. See also
363	[[keystoneos-verification-habits]].
364	
365	**RESOLVED 2026-08-29**: schedule moved 00:30 -> 09:00 in
366	`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.keystone.dailybackup.plist` (PlistBuddy `Set :StartCalendarInterval:Hour 9`,
367	then `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup` + `bootstrap`; live schedule confirmed
368	`Hour => 9, Minute => 0` via `launchctl print`). Old plist kept at `.plist.bak-2026-08-29`. 09:00 was
369	chosen from mount evidence (drive attached 07:31 on 08-29; the 08-17 capture ran 08:05). **Do not
370	verify this by mtime or by exit code** — the only proof is a fresh `_receipts/run-*.txt` on the drive
371	dated 08-30 or later. If receipts still cluster, the drive is not attached at 09:00 and the hour is wrong.
372	
373	`~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` archived to `.errors.log.archived-2026-08-29` and
374	cleared the same day. It held two **still-open** issues, not stale history: memsearch `onnxruntime`
375	import failure (2026-08-22, corroborated by `INDEX full set: Indexed 0 chunks` on 08-28/08-29), and
376	stack-doctor weekly flagging `errors-log`, `flush-stale`, `memfile-full:MEMORY.md` (2026-08-24).
377	
378	**Both cleared by end of 2026-08-29** — stack-doctor returned `ALL CLEAR`: memsearch `search: OK`,
379	`last-flush.json OK (0h ago)`, no `FLUSH_ERROR` in recent dailies, `errors.log: clean`. The
380	`onnxruntime` import failure did not need a reinstall, so **do not** reflexively run
381	`uv tool install --force memsearch` on the next `ETIMEDOUT` — that strips the local flush patch
382	and creates a worse problem. Confirmed here: `memsearch --version` answered instantly (0.4.17) and
383	`pgrep -fc memsearch` was 0, ruling out both a broken binary and the
384	[[milvus-lock-misdiagnosis]] lock-contention pattern.
385	
386	A separate `memsearch-sync: index ETIMEDOUT Nx consecutively` streak ran 6→13 during the afternoon
387	session of 08-29 and then self-cleared. Per the skill's own note, `Indexed 0 chunks` is usually a
388	starved flush pipeline rather than a dead indexer — **check `flush-stale` before touching
389	memsearch**. The streak counter is reset by the nightly backup, so a climbing count mid-session is
390	expected noise unless it survives a backup run. Both cleared by end of 2026-08-29 —
391	stack-doctor returned ALL CLEAR and the thread is closed.
392	
393	Guard trap: shell truncation (`: > file`) anywhere under `$HOME` is blocked by dcg
394	rule `core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-root-home`; `cp /dev/null file` is allowed, and macOS has no
395	`truncate` binary. This file is itself near the `memfile-full` threshold — trim before appending more.
396	
397	## A stalled run with no rsync child = an unanswered macOS access prompt (2026-09-03)
398	
399	`daily-backup.ps1` gates both optional destinations on a bare `Test-Path` with **no timeout**:
400	`Test-Path $GDrive` (section 2a) and `Test-Path $SsdRoot` (section 2b). When macOS has a pending
401	TCC/removable-volume permission prompt for that path, the call blocks **forever** — and because 2a
402	runs before 2b, the SSD capture never happens and no receipt is written.
403	
404	**The tell:** `pwsh` alive in `S`/`SN` state, **zero rsync children**, and the log frozen mid-run.
405	That is not a slow copy — a slow copy always shows an `rsync` process. `ps -axo pid,stat,comm` on
406	macOS marks I/O wait `U`, not `D`; a `D`-state grep finds nothing and proves nothing.
407	
408	**The fix is the human, not the shell — look at the screen for a pending prompt FIRST.** On
409	2026-09-03 both `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-*` and `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` were unresponsive to
410	a plain `ls`. The Drive half cleared after a quit/relaunch of Google Drive, **but Eric was
411	approving access prompts in that same window — the relaunch is unproven and may have done nothing.**
412	Do not treat killing Google Drive as the known fix. The SSD half cleared only when he approved the
413	prompt. **Do not force-unmount CRASHBOX** (exFAT, no journal) — ask first.
414	
415	Probably (unverified): the Claude Code shell and the launchd/reconcile jobs are different TCC
416	principals, so this prompt should not recur for the scheduled runs — but it may fire once per new
417	app that launches the script.
418	
419	**Never re-run without `pkill -f daily-backup.ps1` first.** A hung run is harmless, but several hung
420	runs unblock *together* the moment access is granted and race onto the SSD — the two-writer
421	corruption this whole system exists to prevent.
422	
423	**Timing that matters:** reconcile replays the backup at 07:00 if no `OK` is logged for today, and
424	launchd fires at 09:00 regardless (see "Current state" above). A manual run finishing before 07:00
425	suppresses the replay; one finishing after 07:00 can collide with it.
426	
427	Open gap, not yet fixed: neither `Test-Path` has a watchdog, unlike `Invoke-Rsync`
428	(`$RsyncTimeoutSec = 900`). Worth wrapping both.
429	
430	## `/backup` skill + the completeness signal (2026-09-04)
431	
432	`~/.claude/skills/backup/SKILL.md` is the on-demand path — the launchd job only fires if the
433	Mac is awake at 09:00. Standing routine: plug in CRASHBOX, then type `/backup`.
434	
435	**Job count, not error count, is the completeness signal.** A run with CRASHBOX unmounted
436	reports `OK (0 errors)` with **9 jobs**; the same run with it attached reports **31 jobs**.
437	Never report "backup complete" from a 0-error run without checking `okCount` and naming any
438	skipped target.
439	
440	`repo-push:*` failures are usually a transient `Could not resolve host: github.com`, not a
441	credential or repo problem — commits are already local, so a re-run pushes them. Seen
442	2026-09-04 09:05 on `global-memory` and `skills`; one re-run cleared both.
443	
444	A USB-C drive that powers on but never mounts is almost always a charge-only cable.
445	`diskutil list external` printing nothing at all is the fast check — that is a cable/port
446	problem, not software.
447	
448	Full handoff: `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-04-backup-skill.md`.
449	
450	## Manifest coverage closed + job-count baseline reset (2026-09-09)
451	
452	**The 49 `manifest-unmanaged` folders are gone.** They were never a classification backlog —
453	they were fallout from the GitHub consolidation migration (see [[github-consolidation]]).
454	All 49 added to `backup-manifest.json` in one pass: 47 are git repos with `erash11` remotes
455	(`isRepo:true`, `captureOrphans`/`captureWorkingTree` true, destinations `["ssd","github"]`),
456	and 2 are plain dirs — `_ARCHIVE` (4.3 GB) and `docs` — destinations `["ssd"]` only.
457	`baylor` deliberately omitted from every new entry; it is deprecated and Eric's own newest
458	entry (`DEV/Life-OS`, commit `3444c0b`) already omits it.
459	
460	**`class` is inert.** Grep of `daily-backup.ps1` shows it is read nowhere — only `isRepo`,
461	`captureOrphans`, `captureWorkingTree` and `destinations` drive behavior. The
462	institutional/personal call is documentation. Do not stall a manifest add waiting on it.
463	
464	**A DEV manifest entry never auto-commits or pushes that repo.** `Sync-Repo` is called on a
465	hardcoded list (SecondBrain, global-memory, skills, dotclaude); the manifest loop only calls
466	`Capture-RepoData` (SSD) or `Snapshot-Additive`. Adding 47 project repos was therefore safe
467	with open PRs and dirty trees — verify from source before assuming otherwise.
468	
469	**Job-count baseline is now 76, not 31.** The 2026-09-04 note above (9 = no SSD, 31 = SSD
470	attached) is superseded. Full run with CRASHBOX attached = **76 jobs**. `CAPTURE` only logs a
471	line when a repo has files git does not carry, so 18 log lines with 65 capture jobs is normal —
472	read `okCount`, not the log line count.
473	
474	**Removed 2 dead entries**: `DEV/AI_Analyst` and `DEV/token-dashboard`. Both had moved into
475	`~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/`, which is itself now backed up, so coverage was preserved, not dropped.
476	`DexaProject` stays declared-but-absent on purpose — it lives on Google Drive.
477	
478	**`~/.claude` now tracks session transcripts.** Eric's commit `8a3d55c` (2026-09-09 15:44)
479	un-ignored `projects/`, so the dotclaude repo carries ~368 MB of `.jsonl` transcripts and
480	Tier A memory. This **invalidates the "Tier A memory is NOT in git" trap above** — it now has
481	a third layer. No single file exceeds 40 MB, so pushes succeed; they are just slower.
482	
483	Full handoff: `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-09-backup-manifest-coverage.md`.

---
name: backup-sync-system
description: "Nightly backup/sync architecture and its traps — two-writer root cause, manifest classification rules, Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path, dry-run can't verify writes"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 3db720f8-cca5-4aed-96cd-e7ac4a95ab2d
  modified: 2026-09-13T14:37:48.121Z
---

**Current state (2026-09-03).** Two backup runs happen on most days, and the 09-02 entry was
right about that — but **not** because reconcile hard-codes the backup. The real mechanism,
traced 09-03:

`keystone-reconcile.ps1` is a **generic make-up engine**. It has no mention of `daily-backup` at
all; it loops the registry at `DEV/KeystoneOS/data/jobs.json` and calls
`run-job.ps1 -Job <id> -Trigger reconcile -MadeUp` for any job with no success recorded today.
The `daily-backup` job is in that registry with `reconcile: true`, `graceMinutes: 60`,
`maxAttemptsPerDay: 2`, and `makeupWindow: 07:00-20:00`. Its `successProbe` greps today's
`daily-backup.log` for `daily-backup end: OK`. So:

- **If no successful run is recorded by 07:00, reconcile replays it** → the ~07:00-07:10 run.
- **launchd `com.keystone.dailybackup` fires at 09:00 regardless** → the second run.
- **Run the backup by hand before 07:00 and reconcile skips it** ("already succeeded today").
  Confirmed 09-03: a 06:15 manual run logged `OK` at 06:25, and no 07:00 run happened.

Registry inconsistency worth knowing: `jobs.json` records `schedule.at: "00:30"` while the live
plist fires at 09:00. The make-up window is what actually drives the 07:00 replay, so the stale
`at` has not bitten yet. Still true: `launchctl ... runs = 0` proves nothing — read the log.
Receipts cluster only on days CRASHBOX is attached: a mount gap, not a schedule gap.

**"Scheduled runs cannot push" is NOT yet established — and the two contexts differ.** On
2026-09-03 the **09:00 launchd** run pushed `global-memory` cleanly and ended `OK (0 errors)`:
no `PUSH FAILED`, no `PUSH ERR`. But the **reconcile/`run-job.ps1`** context — which is where the
09-02 07:08 and 08-13 07:00 failures happened — **was not exercised that day**, because the manual
06:15 run pre-empted the replay. Do not read 09-03 as clearing the gap; it only clears launchd.
`daily-backup.ps1:74` no longer swallows the reason: the `Out-Null` was replaced 09-03 with
captured output that logs `REPO <name> : PUSH ERR | <text>` on failure only. **The error text will
only appear on a day nobody runs the backup by hand before 07:00.** Diagnose from that line rather
than assuming a credential gap. `daily-backup.err` is stale (last written 2026-08-06); never read
it as current. Manual remedy after a failed push is still `git -C <repo> push origin main` for
SecondBrain, `.claude/global-memory`, `.claude`.

**SSD layout:** non-repo DEV dirs land in `DEV-nonrepo/`, **not** `DEV/` — there is no `DEV/`
on CRASHBOX (roots are `DEV-nonrepo/`, `DEV-repo-data/`, `DEV-working-tree/`, `claude/`,
`codex/`, `gemini/`, `SecondBrain/`, `_receipts/`). `._`-prefixed files beside every real file
are normal AppleDouble xattr sidecars on exFAT, not corruption or duplication.

The nightly backup is `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (pwsh, launchd

## `snapshot:sessions` — evidence from a live reproduction, 2026-08-14 15:20 (stack-doctor)

Caught the hang in progress and narrowed it. **Root cause still open** — this section is
evidence, not a verdict. Everything below is measured, not inferred:

- **It is a hang, not a slow transfer.** Four rsync processes (client `-a ... codex/sessions/`,
  its `--server` receiver, plus two older receivers) sat at **0.01–0.03 s of CPU across
  34–85 minutes** of wall clock. Zero progress, not slow progress.
- **Nothing is left to copy.** The mirror is **256/256 files** — the previously-missing
  `2026/08/06/rollout-*.jsonl` is present. A complete mirror still hangs.
- **The mount is healthy.** A recursive `find` over the destination returned 256 files
  promptly, and `touch` inside the exact hung directory succeeded instantly. Reads *and*
  writes both work, so this is not a wedged DriveFS/FUSE mount.
- **The wedged processes ignore SIGTERM** (still alive minutes later in `S` state) — they
  are blocked inside a call that neither returns nor delivers signals.
- **Dry runs cannot see it**: `-n` completes clean, live runs hang. Another instance of the
  "`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path" trap above.

### Orphans are a symptom, not the cause

Two `rsync --server` receivers were **orphaned to PPID 1** (started 13:55 and 14:33). It is
tempting to call them the blocker; the timeline refutes it — the **10:31:54 run hung at the
identical point** (last line `SNAP skip (missing): .codex/memories`, no end line) while the
oldest surviving orphan did not exist until 13:55. `kill` on both orphans did not unblock
the live pair either.

Why they accumulate: **`daily-backup.ps1` contains no `pkill` at all** (verified by grep —
do not go looking for one). The anchored `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` belongs to an *ad-hoc
wrapper used interactively in another session*. That pattern matches only the client, whose
`argv[0]` is the full path; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`, so
`pgrep -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` returns the client alone. Every kill-and-retry therefore strands
one more receiver. If that wrapper is reused, match on `-x rsync` or the destination path.

### ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-14 17:00 — it is not rsync

Ran the copy in the foreground with `-avv`, unpiped. It printed ~99 lines of
`... is uptodate` and froze mid-filename. Then:

- `sample <receiver-pid>` showed the process blocked in **`__mmap`** — one frame, not moving.
- `lsof` on it showed FD 5 open on a specific **destination** file:
  `codex/sessions/2026/05/08/rollout-2026-05-08T17-14-58-019e09a8-*.jsonl`.
- **`head -c 512` on that destination file hangs by itself**, with zero rsync processes
  running. A plain read. So the file is unreadable through DriveFS.
- A 44-file sample elsewhere in the same mirror read instantly, so it is **specific files,
  not the mount**.

The files are **DriveFS placeholders** — uploaded to Google, then evicted from the local
cache. Census of the destination on 2026-08-14: 256 files, **122 materialized (48.5 MB on
disk), 134 placeholder-only (240.7 MB logical, 0 bytes local)**. Source is 256/256
materialized. Detect with `stat -f '%b %z'`: blocks==0 with a nonzero logical size means
the content is not local. Reading one forces an on-demand fetch, and that fetch stalls —
which is what blocks `__mmap`. rsync was the victim, not the cause. **Do not chase rsync
flags**; the block happens at open, before any comparison strategy applies.

**This inverts the problem: the backup is fine, the verification is what's broken.** All
256 files are on Google's servers. Nothing is missing. What fails is the *next* run's
attempt to re-read them to confirm they match. Never conclude "the snapshot is broken"
from this failure mode.

Also: `du -sh` on the destination reports the *local cache* (48 MB), not the logical 289 MB.
Both numbers are true and mean different things — do not treat the gap as missing data.

Diagnostic sequence that worked, reuse it: `sample <pid>` for the blocking syscall →
`lsof -p <pid>` for the file it is on → bounded `head -c` on that path to prove the
filesystem, not the tool, is at fault.

**Attempted fix that DID NOT WORK**: pinning `My Drive/Backups` "Available offline" via the
Finder context menu (there is no CLI or xattr for it — the app ships no control surface).
Eric pinned it 2026-08-14 17:30. Result: **one** file materialized, then flat for 5 minutes
(133 placeholders, 49.2 MB, unchanged). Restarting Drive did not help either.

**DriveFS on this Mac is itself unhealthy** — this is the real blocker, not rsync and not
the pin:
- It refused a graceful `osascript quit` for 20s and needed SIGKILL. Its log emitted
  `crashpad ... ThreadsStuck` every 6s. Restarting cleared the stuck threads but nothing else.
- The **download** queue fails, not just uploads: `merger.cc:969:ProcessDownloadEvent` +
  `HandleFailedChange [DownloadMergeQueueItem]`. DriveFS cannot pull content *down*.
- Signs of local DB damage: `item_query_handler.cc:1135:OnGetItemIds Ignoring item
  local-376561 that's missing from ...`.
- NOT quota: 671 GB used of 5.5 TB.

**Do not clear the DriveFS content cache as the remedy.** It converts every materialized
file into a placeholder needing re-download, feeding the exact mechanism that is failing —
122 readable files could become 0. If DriveFS is repaired, do it by signing out and back in
to force a DB rebuild, deliberately, with time to watch it.

### RESOLVED 2026-08-14 — the backup was never broken, the verification was

**Final mechanism**: files Drive has evicted from local cache are placeholders. Fetching a
placeholder through DriveFS is *unreliable* — usually fast, sometimes stalling for tens of
minutes. rsync blocking on such a fetch is the entire "wedge". Proof it is a slow fetch and
not a poisoned file: the file that hung four separate times **now reads instantly**, and its
blocks went 0 → 770,048 — the repeated read attempts eventually completed the fetch. Six
other placeholders read fine first try. Nothing was corrupt.

**`~/.claude/scripts/verify-drive-backup.sh` (`0d2edb5`) is now the way to verify.** It
compares the Drive API's server-side `md5Checksum` against a local md5 — metadata only, no
DriveFS read, batched ~25 names per query. First run on `~/.codex/sessions`:
**256/256 verified, 0 mismatch, 0 missing.** The snapshot that logged `FAILED` for days was
complete and byte-correct the whole time.

Do not "fix" this by deleting Drive copies. Both files that hung were verified byte-identical
to source *before* anything was touched — deleting would have destroyed a good backup to
repair a read path.

**It is plain fetch latency, scaling with file size** — no mystery left. A full read-scan of
all 256 files with a 6s per-file cap: 33 stalled, and those averaged **2,301 KB vs 1,156 KB
for the set overall** (max 15.8 MB). Bigger file, longer fetch. Nothing file-specific,
nothing corrupt. The scan itself moved the mirror from 122 → 230 materialized (48.5 → 161.8 MB
local), which is exactly what "reading materializes it" predicts.

Caution when testing this: **reading a file materializes it**, so any scan warms the cache and
a later run passes for reasons that will not hold once Drive evicts again. Timestamp results
and never treat a post-scan rsync run as a clean verification.

**Google Drive is mirroring `~/DEV` as a device-backup folder named "My Mac"**, including

of the `PRECONDITION_FAILED` storms on `FETCH_HEAD` and the stuck threads in `drive_fs.txt`,
and therefore of the slow placeholder fetches upstream.

Proof (not inference): local `~/DEV/*/.git/FETCH_HEAD` all stamped 18:22:09 while Drive's
server copies read `2026-08-14T23:22:09Z` — same second — and the Drive parent chain resolves
`FETCH_HEAD → .git → DataBase_GPS_Reporting → DEV → My Mac`.

**`OneDrive-Import` was a red herring** — it holds 22 `.git` dirs / 7,292 files, but they are
static archives and do not churn. Don't chase it.

**FIXED 2026-08-14 ~18:28 — Eric removed `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders from your
computer" (keeping the cloud copy). Verified, and it worked:**

- `PRECONDITION_FAILED` 14 → **0**. `ProcessDownloadEvent` errors 11 → **0**.

- Google Drive CPU **64.6% → 0.0%**.
- **End-to-end: 5/5 genuine placeholders (blocks==0) fetched in 2–3s each**, where the same

  the `snapshot:sessions` wedge — the watchdog only bounded it.

## A stalled run with no rsync child = an unanswered macOS access prompt (2026-09-03)

`daily-backup.ps1` gates both optional destinations on a bare `Test-Path` with **no timeout**:
`Test-Path $GDrive` (section 2a) and `Test-Path $SsdRoot` (section 2b). When macOS has a pending
TCC/removable-volume permission prompt for that path, the call blocks **forever** — and because 2a
runs before 2b, the SSD capture never happens and no receipt is written.

**The tell:** `pwsh` alive in `S`/`SN` state, **zero rsync children**, and the log frozen mid-run.
That is not a slow copy — a slow copy always shows an `rsync` process. `ps -axo pid,stat,comm` on
macOS marks I/O wait `U`, not `D`; a `D`-state grep finds nothing and proves nothing.

**The fix is the human, not the shell — look at the screen for a pending prompt FIRST.** On
2026-09-03 both `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-*` and `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` were unresponsive to
a plain `ls`. The Drive half cleared after a quit/relaunch of Google Drive, **but Eric was
approving access prompts in that same window — the relaunch is unproven and may have done nothing.**
Do not treat killing Google Drive as the known fix. The SSD half cleared only when he approved the
prompt. **Do not force-unmount CRASHBOX** (exFAT, no journal) — ask first.

Probably (unverified): the Claude Code shell and the launchd/reconcile jobs are different TCC
principals, so this prompt should not recur for the scheduled runs — but it may fire once per new
app that launches the script.

**Never re-run without `pkill -f daily-backup.ps1` first.** A hung run is harmless, but several hung
runs unblock *together* the moment access is granted and race onto the SSD — the two-writer
corruption this whole system exists to prevent.

**Timing that matters:** reconcile replays the backup at 07:00 if no `OK` is logged for today, and
launchd fires at 09:00 regardless (see "Current state" above). A manual run finishing before 07:00
suppresses the replay; one finishing after 07:00 can collide with it.

Open gap, not yet fixed: neither `Test-Path` has a watchdog, unlike `Invoke-Rsync`
(`$RsyncTimeoutSec = 900`). Worth wrapping both.

name: command-centre
description: "The DEV front door — always-on read-only status page at http://localhost:7373, plus the rules that keep it trustworthy"
metadata:

**Built 2026-08-31.** Closes ARMS gap 5. `~/DEV/CommandCentre/server.py`, served by
`com.keystone.commandcentre` (`RunAtLoad` + `KeepAlive`), own `DESIGN.md`.

**<http://localhost:7373>** — one page answering "is anything broken?": agent
health, backup result, graph progress, logged failures, active projects, and
links to every generated report with its age.

Design rules that must hold, each learned the hard way:

- **Standard library only.** Python 3.14 here is PEP 668-managed, so any
  dependency means a venv to maintain forever. A read-only local page never
  earns that.
- **Rendered fresh per request.** Never cached, never regenerated on a timer. A
  page that can be stale is a page you stop believing — that is exactly why the
  on-demand `project-triage/dashboard.html` never became a front door.
- **A dashboard that contradicts the CLI is worse than no dashboard.** The file
  counter first used `total - len(done)` and disagreed with `gf_remaining.py` by
  13, because the done-list holds entries no longer in the corpus. It now does
  the same **set difference**, and the corpus selection is kept identical across
  `server.py`, `gf_gemini.py` and `gf_remaining.py`.
- **Judge a running service on its PID, not its last exit code.** A `KeepAlive`
  daemon carries the exit code of the instance that *died*, so a restart leaves a
  nonzero code behind permanently. `launchctl list`'s first column is the PID and
  the second is that stale status — reading the wrong column makes a healthy
  service look broken.
- **Live `launchctl` state is the truth**; `run-ledger.json` is shown but never
  allowed to claim a job succeeded. See [[keystoneos-verification-habits]].
- **Every source is optional** — a missing input renders "unknown", never a 500.
- **Bound to `127.0.0.1` only**, which is why it needs no auth. Do not change the
  bind address without adding one. Read-only on purpose: no buttons, so a stray
  browser tab cannot fire an agent. `~/.claude/scripts/skill-button.sh` exists
  for the day buttons are wanted.

**The threat to a localhost service is a web page you visit, not the network.**
Any site your browser opens can make requests to `127.0.0.1`, so binding to
loopback is not a security boundary on its own. **DNS rebinding** is the real
attack: the attacker's domain re-resolves to `127.0.0.1`, their JavaScript
becomes same-origin, and it reads everything. The defence is a **`Host` header
allowlist** — refuse any request whose Host is not a loopback name. Three review
rounds were needed to get the parsing right: compare IPv6 numerically (so
`[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]` is recognised), refuse a second `Host` header rather than
guess, strip exactly one trailing DNS dot, and validate the port range. Also
learned: **curl silently collapses duplicate headers** — prove that guard over a
raw socket.

**An allowlisted name is not an allowlisted file.** `Path.exists()` and
`read_bytes()` follow symlinks, so an exact-path allowlist still served
`/etc/hosts` when the target was swapped for a symlink. Confine the resolved
object too, then **read through the same descriptor you checked** (`O_NOFOLLOW`,
then compare the fd's `(st_dev, st_ino)` to the pre-check `lstat`) — checking a
path and reopening it by name is a check/use race. Close the fd in a `finally`
that catches every exception type, not just `OSError`.

**Any number shown in two places must be computed by identical code.** A page
that contradicts the CLI destroys trust in both. Three separate counters here
had to be aligned four times: set difference not arithmetic, the same corpus
selection, the same skip gates, the same `GF_MAXBYTES` env override — including
its "0 means no cap" convention — and the gate applied to a progress line's
numerator *and* denominator.

**Creating any new `~/DEV/<folder>` breaks the backup immediately** — the manifest
is default-deny, so `daily-backup` exits 1 until the folder is added to
`~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`. Working as designed; just add the entry
in the same turn. The `class` field answers *who keeps this when you leave
Baylor* — `institutional` also copies to Baylor OneDrive ("lost when Baylor
access ends"), `personal` stays yours. See [[backup-sync-system]].

## The `/os` view — added 2026-09-01

A second face over the same sources: **<http://localhost:7373/os>** (page:
`CommandCentre/os.html`, data: `/api/state.json`). `/` is unchanged. Renders
routines, 148 skills, an artifact ring, Second Brain counts, health and projects.
Rationale lives in `DESIGN.md` → "The `/os` view". Backup: `server.py.bak-2026-09-01`.
Design study it came from (video frames + original spec): `CommandCentre/reference/rubric-agentic-os/`.

- **It is read-only, and that is not a gap to fill casually.** It shows which model
  and effort a skill *would* run at; it cannot run one. Run buttons and the model ×
  effort matrix were deliberately **not rendered** — dead controls are worse than
  none. `~/.claude/scripts/skill-button.sh` is the guarded write path for that day.
- **Never add a CORS header to `/api/state.json`, and never open `/os` as
  `file://`.** Same-origin is the only thing keeping the whole state object away
  from any site the browser has open. A `file://` page would need CORS to fetch it
  — that is the trap, not the fix.
- **`/open` allowlists ring files by identical string, recomputed per click** —
  same rule as `LINKS`, never a prefix or subtree test. The ring moves as files are
  written, so a click can 404 when it shifted underneath. That is the correct
  failure; widening the check is how a traversal gets in.
- **The ring must stay capped per folder and per project** (`RING_PER_DIR=2`,
  `RING_PER_PROJECT=6`). Uncapped "40 most recent" gave 22 of 40 from a single
  06:34 generated batch and buried every real deliverable. Verified: capped = 13
  projects.
- **`RING_EXCLUDE` keeps `COG_S2_Position_Reports` off the ring** — those filenames
  carry athlete names and the ring renders filenames as labels, so a glance would
  put named cognitive results on screen. Excluded from this view only.
  See [[s2-cognition-analysis]].
- **`SENSITIVE_PATHS` is module-level now**, shared by `src_graph` and the ring, so
  the graph count and the ring can never disagree about what is off-limits. Still
  must match `gf_gemini.py`.
- **Calendar and email cannot be on this page.** Both live behind MCP servers that
  only exist inside a Claude session; a background HTTP server cannot reach them.
  Caching them would break the never-stale rule the page is built on. They became
  System Health and Projects instead.
- `launchctl kickstart -k` leaves **exit `-15`** on the previous instance. Expected —
  judge it on the live PID, which `src_agents` already does.

- **To verify `/os` renders, use headless Chrome — not the claude-in-chrome
  extension.** The extension returns `Frame with ID 0 is showing error page` for
  `localhost:7373` on both `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, while `curl` gets 200 and
  the server logs nothing. That is the extension's site-permission gate, **not** a
  server fault — do not go hunting for an IPv4/IPv6 bind bug (the server is
  IPv4-only by design, `server.py:878`, and that is not the cause). Working check:
  `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless \
  --disable-gpu --virtual-time-budget=6000 --screenshot=<out>.png \
  --window-size=1440,900 http://127.0.0.1:7373/os`
  **`--virtual-time-budget` is required** — without it the shot fires before the
  `/api/state.json` fetch resolves and every panel reads `LOADING`, which looks
  exactly like a broken board.

Related: [[graphify-semantic-extraction]], [[dev-layout-and-discovery]],
[[s2-cognition-analysis]]

content.content: Updated task #15 status

Quickstart for a page. [Artifact types not listed: a PreToolUse hook may cover Artifact calls — list the types and the design systems with their own calls, so the hook sees them.]

For a plain page, the page-design guidance follows. It is the `artifact-design` skill's own text, so do not load that skill as well. Write the page to a file and publish it in the same message: the two calls run in order.

## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it; always pin an exact version. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Every skill, command and scheduled job in your setup, placed where it belongs in the day, the week and the semester. Windows is the day machine, the Mac the evening machine. Click any command to copy it.

Windows Mac runs itself

Sit down

  • Read the status lines: slate, jobs and milvus, repos behind, next-step buttons. A red job means
  • Every project's next step. Pick one thread.
  • The board, if it isn't open. Focus view shows what's live.

Work blocks

  • One Claude Code session per project, opened in its repo. The board stays open beside it and updates itself. Toolbox below.

Debrief

Windows
  • 10–15 minutes. Three facts for the supervisor log, the project-block question, four reflections.
17:00

Close out

  • Fixes each touched project's card, commits board edits, pushes everything, writes the handoff and STATUS. Ends with "Clear to sign off".

Evening

Mac
  • Pulls everything Windows pushed.

runs itself

runs itself

A scheduled job looks wrong

You're switching machines first, always
A project is driftingPark it on the board, or let Friday's sweep decide
The board won't open prints why; shows a bad registry
Claude Code feels off

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
src = pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name("operating-rhythm.html")

wrapped.write_text('<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">'
                   '<style>body{margin:0}</style></head><body>' + src.read_text(encoding="utf-8") + "</body></html>", encoding="utf-8")
with sync_playwright() as pw:
    b = pw.chromium.launch(executable_path=r"C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe")
    for name, w, scheme in (("desk-light", 1280, "light"), ("phone-dark", 400, "dark")):
        pg = b.new_page(viewport={"width": w, "height": 900}, color_scheme=scheme)
        errs = []
        pg.on("pageerror", lambda e: errs.append(str(e)))
        pg.goto(wrapped.as_uri()); pg.wait_for_timeout(300)
        sw = pg.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth")
        print(name, "scrollWidth", sw, "viewport", w, "errors", errs)
        pg.screenshot(path=str(src.with_name(f"{name}.png")), full_page=(name == "desk-light"))
    b.close()

description: "RETIRED 2026-10-03 — the old localhost:7373 status page (the live project board replaced it); kept for its hard-won localhost security and dashboard-trust rules"
